titulo: Reported questions, commands and reporting verbs
titulo_es: Reported speech: questions, orders and reporting verbs
descripcion_es: Questions and orders in reported speech; verbs like ask, advise, deny, claim, suggest and their structures.
resumen: In reported questions the inversion and the auxiliary do disappear; orders are reported with tell/ask + to + infinitive. Each reporting verb (advise, deny, suggest…) requires its own structure.

explicacion.texto: Reported questions: statement word order (subject + verb), without do/does/did and without a question mark. With yes/no questions we use if or whether. “Where do you live?” → She asked me where I lived. “Are you ready?” → He asked if I was ready.
Orders and requests: tell/ask/order + person + (not) to + infinitive. “Sit down” → He told me to sit down. “Please don't shout” → She asked us not to shout.

filas: advise, encourage, invite, remind, warn, persuade
apologise for, insist on, accuse sb of, blame sb for
She claimed that she had been ill.

items: Suggest never takes person + to: She suggested going / She suggested (that) we (should) go.
Remember to change tenses and references if the reporting verb is in the past: tomorrow → the next day, here → there.
Deny y admit admiten -ing simple o perfecto: He denied having seen her.

ejemplos.frase: The inspector asked me where I had parked the van.
ejemplos.traduccion: El inspector me preguntó dónde había aparcado la furgoneta.

ejemplos.frase: She wanted to know whether the shop opened on Sundays.
ejemplos.traduccion: Quería saber si la tienda abría los domingos.

ejemplos.frase: The doctor warned him not to lift anything heavy.
ejemplos.traduccion: El médico le advirtió que no levantara nada pesado.

ejemplos.frase: My friend suggested taking the coastal road.
ejemplos.traduccion: Mi amigo sugirió ir por la carretera de la costa.

ejemplos.frase: The company claims that its products are fully recyclable.
ejemplos.traduccion: La empresa afirma que sus productos son totalmente reciclables.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: He asked me where did I work.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: He asked me where I worked.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: In a reported question there is no inversion and no did.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: She suggested me to buy a new laptop.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: She suggested that I buy a new laptop.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Suggest does not take person + to; use that + clause or -ing.
For orders use tell + person + to, not say.

ejercicios.frase: "What time does the museum close?" → She asked what time the museum ___.
respuestas: closed
closes
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for reported questions in Rules and key points: statement word order (subject + verb), without do/does/did. The clue is that in the original the auxiliary does marks the question; in the reported question it disappears and its information (present, third person) moves to the verb. With asked in the past, the normal thing is to backshift to closed, but closes is also fine if the opening hours are still the same.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Remove does and use statement word order; the usual choice is to backshift the tense (closed), although closes is possible if it is still true.
ejercicios.traduccion: «¿A qué hora cierra el museo?» → Preguntó a qué hora cerraba (cierra) el museo.

errores_previstos.respuesta: does close
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the reported question the auxiliary does disappears; the verb carries the tense itself: closed or closes.

errores_previstos.respuesta: did close
errores_previstos.explicacion: Did is also a question auxiliary that is not kept in reported speech: closed.

errores_previstos.respuesta: close
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without an auxiliary, the verb must show its tense and person: closed (or closes).

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb.
respuestas: breaking
having broken
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the row “verb + -ing” in the table: deny is followed by -ing. The clue is the reporting verb denied. According to the list in Rules and key points, deny takes a simple -ing form (breaking) or a perfect one (having broken), the latter to stress that the action happened earlier; both are correct.

errores_previstos.respuesta: to break
errores_previstos.explicacion: Deny does not take to + infinitive; it is followed by -ing (breaking).

errores_previstos.respuesta: to have broken
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “negó haber roto”: with deny the perfect form is having broken, not to have broken.

errores_previstos.respuesta: broke
errores_previstos.explicacion: After deny you cannot have a conjugated verb without a subject; use -ing or that + clause.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb.
ejercicios.frase: My boss reminded me ___ (send) the invoice.
respuestas: to send
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “verb + person + to + infinitive” in the table, which includes remind. The clue is the structure reminded me: after the person comes to + infinitive. In Spanish we use “que + subjuntivo” (“me recordó que enviara”), but in English you cannot copy this with that.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi jefe me recordó que enviara la factura.

errores_previstos.respuesta: send
errores_previstos.explicacion: Remind + person is followed by to + infinitive: to send.

errores_previstos.respuesta: sending
errores_previstos.explicacion: Remind does not take -ing in this structure; we say reminded me to send (remind me of sending is not correct).

errores_previstos.respuesta: that I send
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “que enviara”; remind + person + that is used to remind someone of a fact, not to ask for an action. Here the answer is to send.

ejercicios.frase: The police accused him ___ stealing the car.
respuestas: of
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the row “verb + preposition + -ing” in the table: accuse somebody of + -ing. The clue is accused him followed by stealing: the preposition is missing, and in English it is of, just as Spanish says “acusar de”. It is a fixed collocation that is best learnt together with the verb.
ejercicios.traduccion: La policía le acusó de robar el coche.

errores_previstos.respuesta: for
errores_previstos.explicacion: For is used with blame (blame sb for); accuse takes of.

errores_previstos.respuesta: to
errores_previstos.explicacion: Accuse does not take to; the fixed preposition is of.

errores_previstos.respuesta: about
errores_previstos.explicacion: About does not form a collocation with accuse; we say accuse sb of.

ejercicios.frase: She asked me ___ I had ever been to Japan.
respuestas: if
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in Rules and key points: with yes/no questions we use if or whether. The clue is that the original question had no question word (“Have you ever been to Japan?”) and the word order after the gap is a statement order (I had ever been). If here is equivalent to the Spanish interrogative “si”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Yes/no question in reported speech: if/whether.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me preguntó si había estado alguna vez en Japón.

por_opcion.if: Correct: if introduces the reported yes/no question (es: “si había estado”).
por_opcion.that: Incorrect: that introduces statements (said that…), not questions; that is not used with ask.
por_opcion.what: Incorrect: what asks for specific information (es: “qué”); here the expected answer is yes or no.
por_opcion.do: Incorrect: the auxiliary do is not used in reported questions, and besides, the verb is already in the past perfect.

ejercicios.frase: The teacher told the students ___ their phones.
respuestas: to switch off
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for orders: tell + person + to + infinitive. The clue is told the students, which reports an order (“Switch off your phones”). In Spanish it is translated with “que + subjuntivo”, but in English to + infinitive is obligatory.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Tell + person + to + infinitive for orders.
ejercicios.traduccion: El profesor dijo a los alumnos que apagaran los móviles.

por_opcion.to switch off: Correct: tell + person + to + infinitive reports the order.
por_opcion.switch off: Incorrect: to is missing; after tell + person the infinitive takes to.
por_opcion.switching off: Incorrect: tell is not followed by -ing to report orders.
por_opcion.that switch off: Incorrect: a calque of Spanish “que apagaran”; it also lacks a subject. With that you would need a full clause, and for orders to + infinitive is preferred.

ejercicios.frase: He offered ___ me to the airport.
respuestas: to drive
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the row “verb + to + infinitive” in the table, which includes offer. The clue is that me already appears after the gap as the object of drive: offer does not take a person before the infinitive. That is why the structure is offered to drive me (es: “se ofreció a llevarme”).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Offer + to + infinitive, with no person before it.
ejercicios.traduccion: Se ofreció a llevarme al aeropuerto.

por_opcion.to drive: Correct: offer + to + infinitive, with no person before it.
por_opcion.driving: Incorrect: offer is not followed by -ing.
por_opcion.me to drive: Incorrect: offer does not take person + to (that is for advise, invite, etc.); it would also repeat me.

ejercicios.frase: Our guide recommended ___ the museum early.
respuestas: visiting
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “verb + -ing” in the table, which includes recommend next to suggest. The clue is the verb recommended followed directly by the action, with no person. The correct form is recommended visiting. Recommend us to visit is heard and some dictionaries record it, but the rule followed in this card and careful usage prefer -ing or that + clause.
ejercicios.traduccion: Nuestro guía recomendó visitar el museo temprano.

por_opcion.to visit: Incorrect: recommend is not followed by to + infinitive without a person.
por_opcion.us to visit: Incorrect according to the card: recommend, like suggest, is not used with person + to; you would say recommended that we visit. In real usage it is sometimes heard, but it is considered careless.

ejercicios.frase: I asked him where was the station.
respuestas: I asked him where the station was.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule for reported questions: statement word order, with the subject (the station) before the verb (was). The clue is the verb asked: what follows is no longer a direct question, so the inversion “where was the station” disappears. It is the typical mistake listed in the card.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In a reported question the verb goes after the subject.
ejercicios.traduccion: Le pregunté dónde estaba la estación.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I asked him where was the station.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence uncorrected: there is no inversion in a reported question; the subject goes before the verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I asked him where is the station.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It keeps the inversion and also does not backshift the tense; the correct form is where the station was.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I asked him where was the station?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Reported questions have no question mark and no inversion.

ejercicios.frase: She suggested us to take a break.
respuestas: She suggested taking a break.
She suggested that we take a break.
She suggested that we should take a break.
She suggested we take a break.
She suggested we should take a break.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the list: suggest never takes person + to; use -ing (suggested taking) or that + clause (suggested that we take / should take). The clue is us to take, a calque of Spanish “nos sugirió tomar”. All the accepted variants are valid: with -ing, with or without that, and with or without should (the subjunctive take is the most formal form).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Suggest + -ing or + that + clause, never person + to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Sugirió que nos tomáramos un descanso.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She suggested us to take a break.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence uncorrected: suggest does not take person + to + infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She suggested to take a break.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Suggest does not take to + infinitive without a person either; we say suggested taking.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She suggested us taking a break.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With -ing you do not put the person as the object; we say suggested taking or suggested that we take.

ejercicios.frase: He asked me don't tell anyone.
respuestas: He asked me not to tell anyone.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule for negative orders and requests: ask + person + not to + infinitive. The clue is asked me, which reports the request “Don't tell anyone”. In reported speech, don't disappears and the negative is expressed with not before to.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Reported negative order: not to + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me pidió que no se lo dijera a nadie.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He asked me don't tell anyone.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence uncorrected: the negative imperative (don't) is not kept; use not to + infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He asked me not tell anyone.
errores_previstos.explicacion: To is missing: a reported negative request is not to + infinitive (not to tell).

errores_previstos.respuesta: He asked me that I don't tell anyone.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “me pidió que no…”; with ask for requests we use person + not to + infinitive.

ejercicios.enunciado: Put into reported speech, starting with He asked me.
ejercicios.frase: "Did you see the match last night?"
respuestas: He asked me if I had seen the match the night before.
He asked me whether I had seen the match the night before.
He asked me if I had seen the match the previous night.
He asked me whether I had seen the match the previous night.
He asked me if I'd seen the match the night before.
He asked me whether I'd seen the match the night before.
He asked me if I'd seen the match the previous night.
He asked me whether I'd seen the match the previous night.
ejercicios.explicacion: Three rules apply: a yes/no question with if or whether; the auxiliary did disappears and the past simple is backshifted to the past perfect (had seen); and the time reference changes (last night → the night before or the previous night). The pronoun also changes, you → I. That is why there are eight valid combinations (if/whether, had/'d, the night before/the previous night).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: If/whether, past → past perfect and last night → the night before.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me preguntó si había visto el partido la noche anterior.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He asked me did I see the match last night.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It keeps the word order and the auxiliary of the direct question and changes neither the tense nor the time reference.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He asked me if I saw the match last night.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The backshift to the past perfect (had seen) and the change from last night to the night before are missing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He asked me that I had seen the match the night before.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Yes/no questions are introduced with if or whether, not with that.

ejercicios.enunciado: Put into reported speech with the verb advise, starting with The doctor.
ejercicios.frase: The doctor said to me: "You should drink more water."
respuestas: The doctor advised me to drink more water.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the row “verb + person + to + infinitive” in the table, which includes advise. The clue is the advice “You should drink more water”: should disappears because the verb advise itself already expresses the advice, and you becomes me. The structure is advised me to drink.
ejercicios.traduccion: El médico me aconsejó que bebiera más agua.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The doctor advised me to drinking more water.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After to comes the bare infinitive, not the -ing form: to drink.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The doctor advised me drinking more water.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Advise + person is followed by to + infinitive, not by -ing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The doctor advised to me to drink more water.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Advise does not take to before the person: advised me.

ejercicios.enunciado: Put into reported speech with the verb refuse, starting with She.
ejercicios.frase: "I won't sign the contract," she said.
respuestas: She refused to sign the contract.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “verb + to + infinitive” in the table, which includes refuse. The clue is the refusal “I won't sign”: refuse sums up that refusal by itself, so won't disappears and the verb becomes to + infinitive (to sign). It is a good example of how the reporting verb replaces the whole sentence.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Refuse + to + infinitive sums up the refusal.
ejercicios.traduccion: Se negó a firmar el contrato.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She refused signing the contract.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Refuse is followed by to + infinitive, not by -ing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She refused to not sign the contract.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Refuse already contains the negative; adding not reverses the meaning.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She refused that she would sign the contract.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Refuse does not take that + clause; the structure is refused to sign.

respuestas: she asked me where I lived
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule for reported questions: question word (where) + subject (I) + verb (lived), without inversion or did. Before it comes the reporting verb with the person: she asked me. Copying the direct question (where did I live, where lived I) is the mistake to avoid.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Reported question: question word + subject + verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: she asked me where lived I
errores_previstos.explicacion: It keeps the inversion of the direct question; in a reported question the subject goes before the verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: she asked where I lived me
errores_previstos.explicacion: The person being asked goes right after asked.

respuestas: they apologised for the delay
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “verb + preposition + -ing” in the table: apologise for, followed by a noun or -ing. The clue is the word for among the pieces, which always goes with apologise. The order is subject, verb, preposition and complement.

errores_previstos.respuesta: they apologised the delay for
errores_previstos.explicacion: The preposition for goes before its complement: apologised for the delay.

errores_previstos.respuesta: for the delay they apologised
errores_previstos.explicacion: Putting the complement first is a marked and unnatural order; the normal one is subject + verb + for + complement.

descripcion_larga_es: This card extends reported speech to questions, orders and reporting verbs that are more precise than say and tell (advise, deny, refuse, suggest, accuse of…). In reported questions the inversion and the auxiliary do disappear, and each verb requires its own structure. These are very common mistakes among intermediate Spanish speakers and very noticeable in a report or an exam.

contexto.que_es: It is the part of reported speech that reports questions (with the question word or with if/whether and statement word order), orders and requests (tell/ask + person + to + infinitive) and the speaker's intention through specific reporting verbs, each with its own pattern: to + infinitive, person + to, -ing, preposition + -ing or that + clause.
contexto.por_que_importa: Reporting verbs let you sum up precisely what someone said (he refused, she denied, they apologised) instead of always repeating said, which is essential in minutes, reports and news. The mistakes in this card (where did I work, suggested me to) are among the most frequent among B2 Spanish speakers and are heavily penalised in a written exam because they affect the structure of the sentence.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: It is used to report what someone asked, ordered or requested, and to sum up statements with a verb that expresses their function (deny, admit, advise, accuse). The signal is the reporting verb: depending on which one it is, the structure that follows changes. Spanish speakers tend to keep the word order of the direct question and to copy “me sugirió que” as suggested me to.
